title: Platform governance: External innovation preserves gatekeeper power
desc: Explains concentrated power through incentives and architecture while leaving collective costs and future dominance unresolved.

kps.k: Platforms exercise private governance as they become infrastructure for economic and social life.
kps.d: The cluster shifts attention from platforms as innovative intermediaries to their power over access, exchange and institutions. The Platform Society argues that platforms reshape existing institutions rather than create a separate social order. Plantin and colleagues describe a two-way process: platforms acquire infrastructural importance while existing infrastructures adopt platform organisation. The New Utilities connects this position to owners’ power over production and distribution. These are conceptual and historical arguments, supported by illustrative cases rather than quantified causal findings.

qs.q: Platforms, in our view, do not cause a revolution; instead, they are gradually infiltrating in, and converging with, the (offline, legacy) institutions and practices through which democratic societies are organized.
qs.a: The Platform Society: Public Values in a Connective World · Academia · 2018

qs.q: We argue that the rise of digital technologies, in a neoliberal, political, and economic climate, has simultaneously facilitated a “platformization” of infrastructures and an “infrastructuralization” of platforms.
qs.a: Infrastructure studies meet platform studies in the age of Google and Facebook · Academia · 2018

kps.k: Economic incentives and technical architecture jointly explain concentrated platform power.
kps.d: The review of Platform Capitalism attributes to Srnicek an account built around network effects, cross-subsidisation, engagement and data extraction. The Platform Society adds algorithms, ownership, interfaces and user agreements as instruments that organise participation. Its distinction between infrastructural and sectoral platforms locates dependency in a concentrated core dominated, in its account of the Western ecosystem, by Alphabet-Google, Apple, Facebook, Amazon and Microsoft. Srnicek’s advertising, cloud, industrial, product and lean categories instead distinguish business models; they can coexist within one corporation and should not be treated as equivalent to infrastructural position.

qs.q: Economic gains and losses are balanced out as the platform corporation taps on its multiple arms of business.

Now let us first look more closely at the elements that construct a single platform’s anatomy: a platform is fueled by data, automated and organized through algorithms and interfaces, formalized through ownership relations driven by business models, and governed through user agreements.
qs.a: The Platform Society: Public Values in a Connective World · Academia · 2018

kps.k: Platforms enable external innovation while retaining control over its conditions.
kps.d: Plantin and colleagues use mobile operating systems, Facebook and Google Maps to show how third parties build on shared resources while owners control interfaces, collect activity data and impose design changes. This arrangement can reduce duplication and innovation costs but also create lock-in and burdens for developers maintaining products across platforms. Their Open Web comparison qualifies any claim that programmability requires proprietary enclosure: communal standards also support extensibility, and APIs serve governmental open-data initiatives as well as commercial systems.

qs.q: The platform remains a centrally controlled and designed system (often under corporate control), but benefits from the innovations of a large penumbra of third-party developers.
qs.a: Infrastructure studies meet platform studies in the age of Google and Facebook · Academia · 2018

qs.q: The costs of this approach, as platform studies has shown, come in the form of constraints, constant revisions forced by platform updates, and lock-in to the platform’s conception of users, functionality, and design values.
qs.a: Infrastructure studies meet platform studies in the age of Google and Facebook · Academia · 2018

kps.k: Consumer benefits and efficient provision do not settle questions about collective costs, exclusion or discrimination.
kps.d: The sources acknowledge cheaper services, income opportunities, reusable infrastructure and private funding capacity. They nevertheless distinguish these benefits from public-service commitments. The Platform Society uses Airbnb and Coursera to ask who finances shared provision and enforces standards, without quantifying those costs. Plantin and colleagues identify low-income exclusion under fragmented internet provision. The New Utilities argues that consolidated control permits rent extraction and creates vulnerabilities to pricing, racial and geographic discrimination; the supplied passage presents discrimination as a risk, not a measured outcome.

qs.q: Airbnb offers the potential for some individuals to make some money on a spare room and for others to stay in relatively cheap accommodation.
qs.a: The Platform Society: Public Values in a Connective World · Academia · 2018

qs.q: Yet where service is splintered among many for-profit providers, as in the United States, many low- income citizens remain excluded, and their exclusion is both deeply consequential for them and invisible to the dominant culture.
qs.a: Infrastructure studies meet platform studies in the age of Google and Facebook · Academia · 2018

kps.k: The accounts differ in explanatory emphasis and leave the future of platform dominance unsettled.
kps.d: The Platform Capitalism review foregrounds capitalist history and business imperatives; The Platform Society foregrounds contested values and explicitly preserves the agency of users, governments and civil society. This is a difference in emphasis, not a demonstrated direct dispute. The review reports Srnicek’s prediction that platforms will need new surplus-extraction methods or more traditional business forms, and predicts internet fragmentation through enclosure. Neither constitutes an observed outcome. The reviewer’s stronger reinvention-or-collapse interpretation should remain separate from Srnicek’s prediction; its disappointment with the futures discussion comes without a developed alternative.

qs.q: Specifically, by positioning major tech companies as ‘economic actors within a capitalist mode of production’ (3) – instead of cultural or political actors who are informed by cultural values or motivated by the pursuit of power – readers come to understand, with economic clarity, that these companies’ actions are merely reactions to business needs.

Far from being mere technical or economic processes, we emphasize the mutual shaping of technology, economic models, and users: while platform mechanisms filter and steer social interactions, users also define their outcome.2 Understanding the platform society requires a thorough analysis of the ecosystem’s dynamics and the techno-economic and sociocultural practices through which they take shape.
qs.a: The Platform Society: Public Values in a Connective World · Academia · 2018

kps.k: The practical agenda centres on infrastructural accountability and sector-specific public-value choices.
kps.d: The New Utilities proposes public utility thinking to identify and remedy private infrastructural power, but the supplied passage does not specify a regulatory programme. The Platform Society calls for contextual negotiation of fairness, solidarity, privacy, transparency and democratic control, recognising conflicts among these values. Amsterdam’s October 2017 accommodation register illustrates an ongoing local response, not proof of regulatory effectiveness. Together with Plantin and colleagues’ research agenda, this points toward examining who controls interconnection, who bears costs and who loses access across sectors and across local, ecosystem and geopolitical levels.

qs.q: This Part suggests that the public utility framework developed in this Article can help identify and remedy a unique set of problems arising from these firms' position as infrastructural.
qs.a: The New Utilities: Private Power, Social Infrastructure, and the Revival of the Public Utility Concept · Academia · 2018

qs.q: For instance, the need for transparency of data flows is important to help law enforcement but may clash with the privacy protection of users or with other public values such as security, discrimination, or taxing duties.
qs.a: The Platform Society: Public Values in a Connective World · Academia · 2018

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources collectively accept the proposition that platforms enable external participation and innovation while retaining concentrated gatekeeper power, and they materially develop it. Their common explanation combines economic incentives—network effects, data extraction, cross-subsidisation and ecosystem enclosure—with governance through architecture, APIs, algorithms, ownership and user agreements. Plantin and colleagues provide the clearest extension by specifying how owner-controlled interfaces produce lock-in, forced revisions and limited interoperability even as third parties innovate. The New Utilities adds a distinct normative extension, proposing public-utility thinking to address private power once platforms become infrastructure. Material variation lies mainly in emphasis: The Platform Society foregrounds institutions, public values and continuing user and state agency; Platform Capitalism foregrounds capitalist accumulation and competitive pressures; Plantin and colleagues contrast proprietary ecosystems with the Open Web; and The New Utilities prioritises regulatory framing. These sources also acknowledge benefits such as lower innovation costs and efficient provision, and they leave collective costs and future platform dominance unresolved. Their arguments are predominantly conceptual, historical and case-based rather than quantified causal evidence, and this curated set should not be treated as representative of academia generally.

elens.an: The curated 2015–2022 sources collectively accept the proposition that platforms enable outside participation and innovation while retaining gatekeeper control, and they materially develop it. Their common explanation combines economic incentives—network effects, data extraction, cross-subsidisation and enclosure—with architectural controls such as APIs, algorithms, interfaces, terms of service and interoperability restrictions. They also extend the proposition beyond market concentration: as platforms become infrastructure, owner control affects access, public services and public values, motivating sector-specific accountability and, in one source, a public-utility framework. Material variation lies mainly in emphasis rather than direct disagreement. Platform Capitalism foregrounds capitalist competition and monopoly tendencies; The Platform Society stresses institutional change, contested values and continuing user and state agency; Plantin and colleagues most directly explain how third-party innovation, lock-in and central control coexist while noting that open standards can also support programmability; The New Utilities redirects the implications toward regulation without supplying a detailed programme. These are principally conceptual, historical and case-based arguments, not quantified causal findings, and predictions about continued dominance or internet fragmentation remain unsettled.
